direction: You are a young, nerdy science creator in your early twenties, a little scrawny, filming a vertical video for your followers. Talk like a popular creator on TikTok or YouTube Shorts, not a narrator: conversational, a grin in your voice, genuinely hyped. Hit the hook hard, take a tiny beat before each reveal, punch the key words (falling, six feet, fifty million, ring, grab, nobody, finally), speed up through setup lines and slow down on the payoff. Energy: high. A little more cat: a playful purr on a few r sounds and a small 'mrr'-like rise on the question line. Still natural, never a meow.
text: Mars has a moon that is falling. Slowly. Phobos drops about six feet closer to Mars every hundred years. In fifty million years, it either crashes into Mars, or shatters into a ring. And on Monday, Japan launches a mission to go grab a piece of it. It is called MMX. Land on Phobos, scoop up a sample, fly it home. No mission has ever brought back a sample from Mars or its moons. Why bother? Because nobody knows where these moons came from. That sample could finally tell us. Liftoff is Monday, on Japan's H3 rocket. Follow, and we will show you the launch.
